sections.content: The course content is very well organized and carefully designed. The topics are arranged in a logical way, which makes it easy to follow the progression from basic concepts to more advanced materials. The course provides a solid understanding of the key ideas while also giving enough depth to help students develop a more comprehensive view of the subject. I especially appreciate that the course does not simply introduce concepts separately, but helps students understand the connections between different topics. Overall, the materials are informative, relevant, and very useful for both academic study and future research.
sections.teaching: The teaching quality is excellent. The instructor explains the concepts clearly and presents the materials in a well-structured and understandable way. Even when the topics become more complicated, the explanations make it much easier to understand the main ideas and important details. The lectures are well prepared, and the overall pace of the course is appropriate. I also appreciate the effort put into making the course materials clear and accessible. Overall, the instructor is knowledgeable, responsible, and effective in helping students understand the course content. I had a very positive learning experience in this course.
sections.grading: The grading scheme is fair, reasonable, and consistent with the content taught in the course. The assessments provide a good opportunity to review and consolidate the important concepts covered in class. The grading criteria are appropriate for the level of the course, and the assessments are generally aligned with what students are expected to learn. I think the evaluation method gives students a fair chance to demonstrate their understanding of the course materials. Overall, the grading arrangement is well designed and reflects students' learning outcomes appropriately.
sections.workload: The workload is reasonable and well balanced throughout the course. There is enough work to encourage students to review the materials carefully and develop a good understanding of the subject, but it is still manageable with appropriate time planning. The workload is also meaningful rather than unnecessarily heavy, and the time spent on the course contributes directly to understanding the key concepts. Overall, I think the workload is appropriate for a course at this level and provides a good balance between learning, assessment, and independent study.

sections.content: This Knowledge Discovery course systematically covers the complete knowledge extraction pipeline—from raw data to actionable insights—spanning multiple interdisciplinary fields, including data engineering, machine learning, statistics, and domain-specific applications. Rather than merely enumerating algorithms in isolation, the course follows the classic Knowledge Discovery in Databases (KDD) methodology, breaking down the entire knowledge discovery lifecycle into several progressive core stages.
sections.teaching: It is clear.

sections.content: The course offers broad and fairly comprehensive coverage of knowledge discovery and data mining. The topics are arranged in a logical progression, which makes it easier to understand how the different methods relate to one another and when each technique is useful. There is a substantial amount of material to absorb, and the course is not easy, but I learned a great deal and gained a much stronger overall understanding of the field. Overall, the content is definitely better than average.
sections.teaching: Professor Wong organizes the material very well. The lectures are clearly structured, and the explanations usually build from intuition to technical details, so even challenging concepts remain reasonably easy to follow. The course still requires active effort, regular review, and some independent thinking, but the difficulty generally feels productive rather than confusing. The teaching makes a broad and demanding syllabus much more manageable.
sections.grading: The grading is generally reasonable and consistent with the level of the course. The assessments require a real understanding of the concepts rather than simple memorization, so performing well still takes preparation and careful study. Some parts can be challenging, but the expectations feel fair and aligned with what is taught. Overall, the grading is neither unusually generous nor unnecessarily harsh.
sections.workload: The workload is on the heavy side, mainly because the course covers a wide range of topics and expects students to understand them in reasonable depth. Keeping up is much easier with regular study than with last-minute preparation. However, the workload is largely justified by the breadth of coverage and the amount that can be learned, so the course feels demanding but worthwhile rather than busywork.

sections.grading: The final exam covers a substantial amount of material, so students should review the course content carefully and prepare well in advance. Overall, the grading is fair, and students who keep up with the course and study consistently should be able to achieve a good grade.

sections.content:
Course Description
Data mining has emerged as a major frontier field of study in recent years. Aimed at extracting useful and interesting patterns and knowledge from large data repositories such as databases and the Web, the field of data mining integrates techniques from database, statistics and artificial intelligence. This course will provide a broad overview of the field, preparing the students with the ability to conduct research in the field.

Topics
Association
Clustering
Classification
Data Warehouse
Data Mining over Data Streams
Web Databases

sections.content: This course covers basic topics in data mining, including Association, Clustering, Classification, Data Warehouse, Data Streams, Web Databases. The instructor provides detailed slides, so you do not need a reference book. Course materials are maintained here: http://www.cse.ust.hk/~raywong/comp5331
sections.teaching: Raymond was really passionate in teaching. He paid attention to interactions with students and provided in-class exercises on sheets in each topic. Assignments and proposals were graded carefully.
sections.grading:
The breakdown:
Assignment 30%
Project 30%
Final Exam 40%

The grades were OK, not difficult to get a B+, as long as you were dedicated to the assignments and exams.
sections.workload: We had 3 assignments, each with 5 questions. The questions will take time to solve, not very easy. Homeworks were submitted in paper works, normally. The project required up to 4 students to do a survey on a topic, or reimplement ideas in a recently published paper, or do a small research project. A proposal, report and a presentation were needed.

sections.content:
Study tips for finals:

- make sure you memorize the proof for ε-deficient synopsis (this is the only REAL hard thing in this course, so Raymond likes to put it in the final exam)

- go through the algorithms a few times with pen and paper (especially the FT-tree algorithm). They are not hard, but is super tedious and easy to make careless mistakes.

- also, the final exam is not hard because of its content, but because of its short time. So yea, make sure you're familiar with the algorithms.
sections.teaching: Raymond is super nice, has VERY clear notes, and is super responsive to students' questions. One of the best CS professors I've had at UST.
sections.grading:
Fairly good.

Be very careful with the homework, as most people get full marks (i.e. losing a little marks in your homework can have a big impact on your final grade).
sections.workload:
- 3 HW
- No mid term
- 1 project (consists of 1 proposal, 1 final report and 1 presentation)
- 1 final exam

Reasonable workload.

Raymond gives out coupons for people who answer his questions, and that coupon can be used to waive one question in a homework. So try to get coupons as it reduce your workload a fair bit.

Also important to have good teammates for your group project.

sections.content:
Contents include Association Rule Mining, Clustering, Classification, Data Stream, Data Warehousing, Web Database, Multi-criteria Decision Making.

Compared to the UG data mining course, this course is naturally more difficult. It covers the proof of the important concepts/equations as well as some math (e.g. Information Theory), which is necessary.

This course also clearly distinguishes itself from Machine Learning course (e.g. only cover Neural Networks and SVM very briefly), which is good.
sections.teaching:
Raymond's teaching is very good. He comes to classes well prepared every time. His teaching materials and homework assignments cover computations, writing proof and reasoning with some math (e.g. proofing an equation by induction), and applying some engineering tricks to solve new problems. I personally learned a lot from this course.

His questions required no rote memorization at all, involved no ambiguous definition, which I think is good.
sections.grading:
30% on Homeworks (three in total)
30% on the Project
40% on Final Exam

The grading is good. I got full marks in all three HWs, 95.5/100 in final (mean 78.xx), project unknown, and received A+.
sections.workload:
The HWs requires some ingenious thinking (applying the  algorithms covered in lectures smartly) and is handleable as long as some quality time is put in.

The project accounts for the most in-semester workload. But since we had almost entire freedom in the project (do research/implementation/survey on any Database/Data Mining/Machine Learning/Information Retrieval paper), doing the project is not intimidating. According to the professor himself, the workload of the project totally depends on the students themselves, so its quite 'elastic'.

sections.workload:
The most workload lies on the group project. Choose a paper from a top conference as the baseline and conduct a survey (maxmimum 80% project mark achievable) / implementation (maximum 90% project mark achievable) / research (maximum 100% project mark achievable).
To perform good in the final exam, it is a good idea to review all exercises and homeworks because most of the final questions were basic as a result of the in-class election.
